00A.idea: General topics that cut across all of math(s), like recreational math(s), popular articles and math(s) education material.
00A.entry: Pick any classic recreational puzzle, such as the Monty Hall problem, and let kids play it 20 times with cups and a coin to see who should switch.

00B.idea: Bookkeeping: conference proceedings and collected volumes, not a topic in its own right.

01A.idea: Math(s) has a history: ideas were discovered by real people, in many cultures, often slowly and with mistakes along the way.
01A.entry: Multiply 23 by 47 the ancient Egyptian way, by doubling and adding, then compare it with the method you learned in school.

03A.idea: What is a proof, what makes math(s) true, and are mathematical objects discovered or invented?
03A.entry: Debate: if nobody had ever counted, would 7 still be prime? Then read the liar sentence "This sentence is false" and decide if it is true.

03B.idea: Logic studies which arguments are valid by their form alone, regardless of what the words mean.
03B.entry: Knights always tell the truth, knaves always lie. A says "B is a knave." B says "We are both knights." Who is who? Build a truth table to check.

03C.idea: Model theory asks which structures make a set of rules true, and what the rules alone can and cannot force.
03C.entry: Write three rules for a "friendship" relation, then find two very different groups of people (or dot pictures) that both obey every rule.

03D.idea: Some well-posed yes/no questions can never be answered by any computer program, no matter how clever.
03D.entry: Play the halting game: a program that does the opposite of what a predictor says about it. Show by a short story why no perfect predictor can exist.

03E.idea: Set theory builds all of math(s) from collections, and shows some infinities are strictly bigger than others.
03E.entry: Try to list every infinite string of 0s and 1s. Flip the diagonal digits of any list to build a string that is missing: Cantor's diagonal trick.

03F.idea: Proof theory studies proofs themselves as objects, and constructive math(s) asks for proofs that actually build what they claim exists.
03F.entry: Prove there exist irrational a, b with a^b rational using root 2 to the root 2, then notice the proof never tells you which case holds.

03G.idea: Algebraic logic turns logical reasoning into algebra, so AND, OR and NOT obey equations you can calculate with.
03G.entry: Let 1 mean true and 0 false. Check that AND is multiplication and that NOT x is 1 - x, then simplify a knight-and-knave puzzle by algebra.

03H.idea: Nonstandard models add infinitely small and infinitely large numbers to ordinary numbers while keeping all the usual rules working.
03H.entry: Is 0.999... less than 1 by an infinitely tiny amount? Argue both sides, then see how a world with infinitesimals makes the slope of x squared exactly 2x.

05A.idea: Counting cleverly: find how many arrangements there are without listing them all.
05A.entry: How many ways can you climb 10 stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time? Count small cases, spot the Fibonacci pattern, and explain why it works.

05B.idea: Designs are arrangements where every pair or group appears together exactly the same number of times.
05B.entry: Arrange 9 kids into groups of 3 over 4 days so every pair of kids shares a group exactly once (a small Kirkman schoolgirl puzzle). The card game Dobble works the same way.

05C.idea: Graph theory studies dots joined by lines, capturing networks, maps, friendships and routes.
05C.entry: Try to draw the envelope shape without lifting your pencil or retracing a line. Count lines at each corner to predict when it is possible, as Euler did for Königsberg's bridges.

05D.idea: Extremal combinatorics asks how big something can be before a pattern is forced to appear.
05D.entry: Among any 6 people, three are mutual friends or three are mutual strangers. Colour the 15 lines between 6 dots red or blue and try to avoid a single-coloured triangle.

05E.idea: Algebraic combinatorics uses algebra, symmetry and polynomials to count and to reveal hidden structure in arrangements.
05E.entry: How many different necklaces of 4 beads in 2 colours are there if rotations count as the same? Count by averaging over the 4 rotations.

06A.idea: An order says when one thing comes before another, even if some pairs cannot be compared at all.
06A.entry: Draw the getting-dressed diagram: socks before shoes, underwear before trousers. Find every valid dressing order and notice some items are incomparable.

06B.idea: A lattice is an order where every two elements have a best common lower bound and a best common upper bound.
06B.entry: Draw the divisors of 12 in layers, with a line up when one divides the next. For any two, find their gcd below and their lcm above.

06C.idea: Modular and complemented lattices are orders with extra balance rules, like those followed by subspaces in geometry.
06C.entry: List the subspaces of the plane: just the origin, every line through it, and the whole plane. Check that each line has a "complement" line, and many choices work.

06D.idea: Distributive lattices are orders where meet and join distribute over each other, just like AND and OR do.
06D.entry: Using divisors of 30 with gcd and lcm, check that gcd(a, lcm(b,c)) equals lcm(gcd(a,b), gcd(a,c)) for several triples. Then find a lattice drawing where it fails.

06E.idea: Boolean algebra is the algebra of true and false, or of subsets, and it runs every digital circuit.
06E.entry: Shade Venn diagrams to check that NOT (A or B) is the same as (NOT A) and (NOT B). Then build that rule from switches in a light circuit.

06F.idea: Ordered algebraic structures combine arithmetic with an order, asking which ordering rules fit together with adding and multiplying.
06F.entry: Show that the clock numbers mod 5 cannot be ordered so that adding 1 always makes things bigger: going round five times returns you to the start.

08A.idea: Universal algebra studies any set with operations, looking for laws shared by numbers, symmetries, words and more.
08A.entry: Invent an operation on {rock, paper, scissors}: the winner of the pair. Test whether it is commutative and associative, and compare with ordinary addition.

08B.idea: A variety is the family of all structures obeying the same list of equations, such as all groups or all lattices.
08B.entry: Pick the single law a*b = b*a. Find three very different things that obey it (adding numbers, mixing paints, taking the max) and one that fails (subtraction).

08C.idea: Other kinds of algebraic systems: partial operations, structures with relations as well as operations, and more general ones.
08C.entry: Colour mixing as a partial operation: some pairs combine and some are not allowed. Make a table and ask which algebra laws still make sense.

11A.idea: The basic structure of whole numbers: primes, divisibility, remainders and the fact that every number factors uniquely into primes.
11A.entry: Run the sieve of Eratosthenes on 1 to 100 and circle the primes. Then explain why the divisibility test for 9 works by adding digits.

11B.idea: Number sequences and special sets of integers, and the patterns, growth and recurrences they follow.
11B.entry: Write Fibonacci numbers and divide each by the one before. Watch the ratios settle near 1.618, and check every third Fibonacci number is even.

11C.idea: Polynomials and matrices with whole-number or rational entries, and what number-theoretic rules they obey.
11C.entry: Can 2x squared + 3x + 7 be factored using whole numbers? Use the rational root test: only a few candidates like 1, 7, 1/2, 7/2 need trying.

11D.idea: Diophantine equations ask for whole-number solutions to equations, which can be surprisingly hard or impossible.
11D.entry: With only 5p and 7p stamps, what postage amounts can you make? Find the largest you cannot (23p) and show why everything bigger works.

11E.idea: Quadratic forms ask which numbers can be written as expressions like x squared + y squared, and how such forms behave.
11E.entry: Which numbers up to 50 are a sum of two squares? Mark them and spot that primes leaving remainder 3 when divided by 4 never appear.

11F.idea: Automorphic forms are functions with an enormous amount of symmetry, and they secretly encode deep number patterns.
11F.entry: Look at an Escher-style tiling of the disc by triangles. A modular form is a function that repeats across every tile; colour a few tiles to see the symmetry.

11G.idea: Arithmetic geometry studies rational points on curves, using the shape of a curve to understand its whole-number or fraction solutions.
11G.entry: Find all rational points on the circle x squared + y squared = 1 by drawing lines of rational slope through (-1, 0). Out pop the Pythagorean triples.

11H.idea: The geometry of numbers counts and uses lattice points, the dots with whole-number coordinates, inside shapes.
11H.entry: On dot paper draw a polygon with corners on dots. Count interior and boundary dots and check Pick's formula: area = interior + boundary/2 - 1.

11J.idea: How well can irrational numbers be approximated by fractions, and which numbers are not roots of any polynomial?
11J.entry: Find fractions close to pi with small denominators. Why is 22/7 so good, and 355/113 astonishingly good? Use continued fractions on a calculator.

11K.idea: Studies how sequences spread out modulo 1, and which digit patterns are typical for almost every number.
11K.entry: Write the first digits of 2, 4, 8, 16, ... up to 2^30 and tally them. Leading 1s appear about 30% of the time: Benford's law.

11L.idea: Exponential and character sums add up spinning arrows whose angles depend on numbers, and measure how random those numbers look.
11L.entry: Draw arrows of length 1 at angles n squared times 10 degrees for n = 1 to 36, joined head to tail. Watch a curly pattern rather than a random walk.

11M.idea: Zeta and L-functions package information about primes into a single function whose zeros control how primes are spread out.
11M.entry: Add 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + ... on a calculator and watch it approach pi squared over 6, a surprise linking squares to circles.

11N.idea: How primes and divisors are distributed among the integers, such as roughly how many primes lie below a given number.
11N.entry: Count primes below 100, 1000 and 10000 (from a table) and compare with n divided by the natural log of n. The ratio creeps towards 1.

11P.idea: Additive number theory asks how numbers can be written as sums, such as sums of primes, squares or smaller whole numbers.
11P.entry: List all ways to write 1 to 7 as sums of positive whole numbers, ignoring order. Check that partitions into odd parts equal partitions into distinct parts.

11R.idea: Algebraic number theory enlarges the integers, for example with square roots, and studies how primes factor in these bigger number systems.
11R.entry: In numbers a + b root(-5), show 6 = 2 x 3 = (1 + root(-5))(1 - root(-5)). Unique factorisation breaks, and math(s) needed ideals to fix it.

11S.idea: Local fields like the p-adic numbers measure size by divisibility by a prime, so huge powers of p count as tiny.
11S.entry: In 10-adic arithmetic, check that ...9999 + 1 = 0, so ...9999 behaves like -1. Then find the last digits of a number whose square ends in itself, like 76.

11T.idea: Finite fields are number systems with finitely many elements where you can add, subtract, multiply and divide, like clock arithmetic mod a prime.
11T.entry: Make a multiplication table mod 7 and find every number's inverse. Then try mod 6 and see some numbers have no inverse.

11U.idea: Logic meets number theory: which questions about whole numbers can be decided by an algorithm, and which cannot.
11U.entry: Hilbert asked for a recipe to decide if any polynomial equation has whole-number solutions. Try a few, then learn the 1970 answer: no recipe can exist.

11Y.idea: Computational number theory finds fast algorithms for primes, factoring and big number calculations.
11Y.entry: Find 3 to the power 100 mod 7 by hand using repeated squaring, in under ten steps, and see why computers can check huge primes quickly.

11Z.idea: Applications of number theory to the real world, such as codes, check digits, cryptography and music.
11Z.entry: Check the last digit of a book's ISBN using the weighted sum mod 11, then show that swapping two neighbouring digits always gets caught.

12D.idea: Real and complex number fields, especially where polynomial roots lie and why every polynomial has complex roots.
12D.entry: Sketch y = x cubed - 3x + 1 and count real roots by sign changes. Then plot complex cube roots of 1 as points round a circle.

12E.idea: A field is any number system where the four operations work; this section studies fields in general and polynomials over them.
12E.entry: Build a 4-element field from {0, 1, a, a+1} with a times a = a + 1 and all coefficients mod 2. Fill in the full multiplication table.

12F.idea: Field extensions add new numbers like root 2 to a field and track the symmetries of roots; this is Galois theory.
12F.entry: Why can't you trisect 60 degrees with ruler and compass? Constructible lengths only use square roots, but trisecting needs a cube root. Try it and fail.

12G.idea: Homological methods use layered algebraic bookkeeping to measure how field extensions fit together, and what obstructs certain constructions.
12G.entry: Honestly very abstract. Best glimpse: the carry in adding two-digit numbers is a "cocycle", the bookkeeping that glues the digit place values together.

12H.idea: Differential algebra treats differentiation as an algebraic operation, and asks which functions have antiderivatives in elementary terms.
12H.entry: Differentiate x e^x and x squared e^x, then guess an antiderivative of x cubed e^x. Learn that e^(-x squared) has no elementary antiderivative at all.

12J.idea: Topological fields are number systems where you also have a notion of closeness, like reals or p-adics.
12J.entry: Compare two distance rules on fractions: the usual one, and "close if the difference is divisible by a high power of 2". Under the second, 1, 3, 7, 15, 31 approach -1.

12K.idea: Generalisations of fields relax some rules, for example allowing multiplication that is not commutative or associative.
12K.entry: Rotate a book 90 degrees about two axes in each order. Different results show multiplication of rotations need not commute, which quaternions capture.

12L.idea: Connections between field theory and logic, such as which statements about fields can be decided mechanically.
12L.entry: Tarski showed any statement about real numbers using +, x and < can be settled by an algorithm. Test one: does every cubic have a real root?

13A.idea: Commutative rings are number systems where you can add, subtract and multiply in any order, but maybe not divide.
13A.entry: Compare clock arithmetic mod 12 with ordinary integers: in mod 12, 3 x 4 = 0 even though neither is 0. Find all such zero divisors.

13B.idea: Ring extensions study what happens when you enlarge a ring by adding new elements, like adding i to the integers.
13B.entry: Explore Gaussian integers a + bi on a grid. Show 5 = (2 + i)(2 - i), so 5 is no longer prime once i is allowed.

13C.idea: Ideals and modules: an ideal is a set closed under adding and multiplying by anything, like all multiples of 6.
13C.entry: Show that numbers of the form 12a + 18b are exactly the multiples of 6. The ideal generated by 12 and 18 is just the multiples of the gcd.

13D.idea: Homological methods measure how far a ring or module is from simple, using chains of maps and how badly they fail to be exact.
13D.entry: Honestly abstract. Glimpse: a counting puzzle where each stage's output is the next stage's input, and Euler's V - E + F = 2 appears as an alternating sum.

13E.idea: Chain conditions say you cannot climb forever: every increasing chain of ideals must stop, which keeps rings manageable.
13E.entry: Start with multiples of 64, then 32, 16, ...: each set contains the last. Why must this chain of multiples stop after a few steps in the integers?

13F.idea: Special rings with good arithmetic, such as those with unique factorisation, Euclidean division or polynomial structure.
13F.entry: Do long division with remainder for Gaussian integers on a grid: find the nearest lattice point to a/b. It always lands within distance less than 1.

13G.idea: Integral domains are rings with no zero divisors, where ab = 0 forces a = 0 or b = 0, like ordinary integers.
13G.entry: Solve x squared = x in ordinary numbers (0 and 1) and in mod 6 (also 3 and 4). Zero divisors create the extra answers.

13H.idea: Local rings focus on one point, ignoring everything far away, like looking at a curve through a microscope.
13H.entry: Zoom into the curve y squared = x cubed + x squared at the origin on graphing software. Near 0 it looks like two crossing lines y = x and y = -x.

13J.idea: Topological rings add a notion of closeness to rings, like power series where higher powers count as smaller.
13J.entry: Treat 1/(1 - x) as 1 + x + x squared + ... and multiply by (1 - x) term by term. Everything cancels, so the infinite sum really is an inverse.

13L.idea: Applications of logic to commutative algebra, using ideas like ultraproducts to transfer results between number systems.
13L.entry: Honestly hard. Glimpse: a fact true mod every large prime, like "x squared + 1 = 0 has a solution for half the primes", hints at a statement about all fields.

13M.idea: Finite commutative rings: number systems with finitely many elements, like clock arithmetic mod n.
13M.entry: Write the multiplication tables mod 4 and mod 5 side by side. Find which numbers have inverses in each, and link it to sharing factors with n.

13N.idea: Differential algebra in commutative rings treats taking derivatives as an algebraic rule, with the product rule as the key axiom.
13N.entry: Define D on numbers by D(prime) = 1 and D(ab) = aD(b) + bD(a). Compute the "arithmetic derivative" of 6, 12 and 30.

13P.idea: Computational commutative algebra solves polynomial systems by systematic elimination, such as Gröbner bases.
13P.entry: Solve x + y = 5 and xy = 6 by eliminating y to get a single polynomial in x. That elimination step is the seed of Gröbner bases.

14A.idea: Foundations of algebraic geometry: shapes defined by polynomial equations, studied through the algebra of those equations.
14A.entry: Graph x squared + y squared = 25 and list its whole-number points. The shape and the equation are two views of the same object.

14B.idea: Local theory zooms in on one point of a polynomial curve or surface, especially points where it crosses or forms a cusp.
14B.entry: Plot y squared = x cubed and y squared = x squared (x + 1). One has a sharp cusp at the origin, the other a crossing. Describe each by zooming in.

14C.idea: Cycles are formal sums of curves and points on a shape, used to count intersections in a consistent way.
14C.entry: Count how many points two straight lines meet in. Then a line and a circle, then two circles. Guess the rule: degrees multiply (Bézout).

14D.idea: Families of shapes that vary continuously, like a curve that changes as a parameter moves, and what happens when they degenerate.
14D.entry: Graph xy = t for t = 4, 1, 0.1 and 0. The hyperbola squashes into two crossing axes at t = 0. Sketch the whole family.

14E.idea: Birational geometry studies shapes up to transformations that may squash or blow up a few points, to find the simplest model.
14E.entry: Draw lines through one point of a circle to all others. Each slope gives exactly one circle point, so the circle is "the same" as a line, except one point.

14F.idea: Cohomology in algebraic geometry counts holes and other hidden features of polynomial shapes, often via clever counting.
14F.entry: Count solutions of y squared = x cubed + 1 mod p for p = 5, 7, 11. Weil's insight: such counts are governed by the shape's holes.

14G.idea: Arithmetic problems on polynomial shapes: finding rational or whole-number points, and how many there can be.
14G.entry: On y squared = x cubed - 2 start from (3, 5). Draw the tangent there, find where it hits again, and get a new rational point (129/100, 383/1000), as Fermat did.

14H.idea: Algebraic curves, the solution sets of one polynomial in two variables, classified by their degree and number of holes.
14H.entry: On a graphing app draw y squared = x cubed - x + c for several c. See the curve split into one or two pieces, and count where lines hit it.

14J.idea: Surfaces and higher-dimensional shapes cut out by polynomials, and how to classify them.
14J.entry: Build a hyperboloid of one sheet from straws between two paper circles twisted apart. A curved surface made of straight lines.

14K.idea: Abelian varieties are polynomial shapes that are also groups: you can add their points, the simplest being elliptic curves.
14K.entry: On y squared = x cubed - x + 1, add two points by drawing the line through them, finding the third crossing and reflecting. Check P + Q = Q + P.

14L.idea: Algebraic groups are symmetry groups defined by polynomial equations, like rotations or invertible matrices.
14L.entry: Rotation matrices with entries cos and sin satisfy a squared + b squared = 1. Multiply two and check you get another rotation, a group living on a circle.

14M.idea: Special varieties, like Grassmannians and toric varieties, are very symmetric polynomial shapes that can be described by pictures and counting.
14M.entry: Toric glimpse: list the monomials x^a y^b z^c with a + b + c = 3 as dots in a triangle. The triangle of dots is the picture of a toric surface.

14N.idea: Enumerative geometry counts geometric objects, like how many lines meet four given lines, and projective geometry adds points at infinity.
14N.entry: Two lines always meet in projective geometry: parallel railway tracks meet at the horizon. Draw a perspective picture with a vanishing point.

14P.idea: Real algebraic geometry studies polynomial shapes over the real numbers, including how many ovals a curve can have and where polynomials are positive.
14P.entry: Graph (x squared - 1)(y squared - 1) = c for c small positive and negative. Count the separate ovals and pieces as c changes.

14Q.idea: Computational algebraic geometry: algorithms to compute with polynomial shapes, such as finding intersections or simplifying equations.
14Q.entry: Find where the circle x squared + y squared = 25 meets the line y = x + 1 by substitution. Then let a graphing app check the two points.

14R.idea: Affine geometry studies polynomial maps of ordinary space, including the famous unsolved question of when they can be reversed.
14R.entry: Check that (x, y) goes to (x, y + x squared) can be undone by another polynomial map. The Jacobian conjecture asks when this always happens.

14T.idea: Tropical geometry replaces + with max and x with +, turning curved polynomial shapes into piecewise straight graphs.
14T.entry: Do tropical arithmetic: 3 "plus" 5 = 5 and 3 "times" 5 = 8. Graph the tropical line max(x, y, 0) and see three rays meeting at a point.

15A.idea: Many problems are just systems of straight-line equations, and matrices let us solve them all at once and see when answers exist.
15A.entry: Lights Out on a 3x3 grid: pressing a button flips it and its neighbours. Work out which presses turn every light off; pressing twice undoes, so it is algebra mod 2.

15B.idea: Matrices with special patterns, like magic squares, permutation grids or stochastic tables, behave in special, predictable ways.
15B.entry: Write a 3x3 table of chances for tomorrow's weather given today's (rows add to 1). Multiply it by itself to forecast two days ahead and watch rows settle to the same numbers.

16B.idea: A ring is any number system where you can add and multiply with the usual rules, except multiplication might not commute.
16B.entry: Clock arithmetic mod 12: make the full multiplication table, spot that 3 times 4 is 0, and ask which numbers have a partner that multiplies to 1.

16D.idea: Ideals are the multiples of something inside a number system, and they let you build new number systems by ignoring those multiples.
16D.entry: List all even numbers, then all multiples of 3. Show that a multiple of 3 times anything is still a multiple of 3, which is why clock arithmetic mod 3 works.

16E.idea: Homological methods measure how far a structure is from being simple by building chains of approximations and counting what is left over.
16E.entry: Best glimpse: the chain where each step's output is used up by the next (like 0 to 2Z to Z to Z/2 to 0); check every arrow's image is exactly the next arrow's zero set.

16G.idea: Representation theory studies an abstract algebra by making it act on arrows and dots, so it becomes a picture of linear maps.
16G.entry: Draw two dots with one arrow and put a number of beads on each dot; classify all ways to connect beads by strings, finding only three basic building blocks.

16H.idea: Some number systems are built like vectors with a multiplication, and the best known new one is the quaternions.
16H.entry: Hamilton's quaternions: use the rules i times j is k but j times i is minus k. Multiply small combinations and see that order matters, just like turning a book.

16K.idea: A division ring lets you divide by anything nonzero even when multiplication does not commute, and there are surprisingly few of them.
16K.entry: Check that every nonzero number mod 7 has an inverse, but mod 6 some do not. Then find the inverse of a quaternion by flipping the signs of i, j, k.

16L.idea: A local ring has exactly one way to fail to be invertible, so it zooms in on behaviour near a single point.
16L.entry: Work mod 9: list which numbers have inverses. Notice the non-invertible ones are exactly multiples of 3, one single family.

16N.idea: A radical collects the elements that are nearly zero, such as things that become zero when multiplied by themselves enough times.
16N.entry: Mod 8, find numbers whose powers eventually hit 0 (2, 4, 6). Show that adding two such numbers gives another one.

16P.idea: Finiteness conditions ask whether chains of ever bigger pieces must stop, which is what makes many proofs about algebra terminate.
16P.entry: Start with multiples of 64, then 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: each set contains the last. Why must every such growing chain of 'multiples of' sets stop?

16R.idea: Some non-commuting systems still obey a hidden polynomial rule, like 2x2 matrices satisfying a fixed identity, which tames their behaviour.
16R.entry: For 2x2 matrices A and B, compute AB minus BA several times and check that its square is always a plain number times the identity matrix.

16S.idea: New rings are made from old ones: polynomials, matrices with ring entries, or rings where variables do not commute.
16S.entry: Build 'twisted polynomials' where x times a number n equals 2n times x. Multiply (x+1)(x+1) and compare with the ordinary answer.

16T.idea: Hopf algebras are structures that can both combine and split things, which is the algebra behind symmetry and quantum groups.
16T.entry: Count ways to split a word into two pieces in order (ABC: '', ABC; A, BC; ...). Then shuffle two words together, and see splitting and shuffling fit like opposite operations.

16U.idea: Special elements of a ring, like units that can be undone, idempotents that square to themselves, and zero divisors, reveal its structure.
16U.entry: Mod 10, find all x with x times x equal x. You get 0, 1, 5, 6. Why do 5 and 6 add to 1 and multiply to 0?

16W.idea: Rings with extra structure, like a grading by degree or a symmetry such as complex conjugation, carry more information than bare rings.
16W.entry: Sort polynomial terms by degree and check the degree of a product is the sum of degrees. Then check conjugating a product of complex numbers reverses nicely.

16Y.idea: Loosening the rules of rings gives new systems, like semirings where you cannot subtract, which still have useful algebra.
16Y.entry: Tropical arithmetic: let 'plus' mean min and 'times' mean ordinary plus. Find the shortest route through a small road map by doing a 'matrix multiplication' with these rules.

16Z.idea: Computers can decide questions about non-commuting algebra by rewriting expressions into a standard form.
16Z.entry: Rewriting game: in words of a and b, the rule is 'ba becomes ab'. Rewrite any word to its standard form and count how many standard forms of length 4 exist.

17A.idea: Nonassociative systems drop the rule that (xy)z equals x(yz), so the order of grouping changes the answer.
17A.entry: Rock paper scissors 'winner' operation: compute (rock, paper) then scissors, versus rock with (paper, scissors). Different results, so grouping matters.

17B.idea: Lie algebras capture tiny symmetries, measuring how much doing two small moves in different orders fails to agree.
17B.entry: Hold a book: rotate a quarter turn forward then a quarter turn sideways, versus the reverse. The difference between the two outcomes is a third rotation.

17C.idea: Jordan algebras use the symmetric product (xy+yx)/2, the multiplication that matches how quantum measurements combine.
17C.entry: Take two 2x2 matrices, compute (AB+BA)/2 and AB. Check the first keeps symmetric matrices symmetric while the second usually does not.

17D.idea: Other nonassociative systems include the octonions, an eight-dimensional number system where even grouping order matters.
17D.entry: Use the Fano plane picture (seven points, seven lines) as a multiplication table for octonion units and find three units where (ab)c differs from a(bc).

18A.idea: Category theory studies math(s) through arrows between objects, focusing on how things connect rather than what they are made of.
18A.entry: Draw towns as dots and one-way roads as arrows; any two roads end-to-start join into a route. Check route joining is associative and every town has a 'stay put' route.

18B.idea: Many familiar worlds, like sets with functions or shapes with continuous maps, are particular categories with their own patterns.
18B.entry: Count all functions from a 2-element set to a 3-element set (9) and from 3 to 2 (8). Which ones can be undone from the other side?

18C.idea: Algebraic theories, like 'groups' or 'monoids', can themselves be treated as mathematical objects that generate their examples.
18C.entry: List all words using letters a, b that you can make by sticking words together. This 'free' set is the most general monoid; any example is a squashed copy of it.

18D.idea: Categories can carry extra structure, such as ways to combine objects side by side or arrows between arrows.
18D.entry: Draw string diagrams: boxes with wires in and out. Show that putting two boxes side by side then stacking gives the same as stacking then side by side.

18E.idea: Categorical algebra studies limits, exactness and adjunctions: universal best approximations that appear everywhere in math(s).
18E.entry: Rounding as a 'best approximation': for real x, the floor is the largest whole number at most x. Check that n at most floor(x) exactly when n at most x.

18F.idea: Gluing local information into global information, as with sheaves, is captured by categories attached to spaces.
18F.entry: Patch a map: each friend knows the temperature in overlapping parts of a town. When do their readings agree on overlaps so they glue into one town-wide map?

18G.idea: Homological algebra measures hidden holes and obstructions using chains of maps where doing two steps in a row gives zero.
18G.entry: Count vertices minus edges plus faces on a cube, a donut-shaped block and a tetrahedron. The answer detects holes, the first shadow of homology.

18M.idea: Monoidal categories and operads describe all the ways to combine several inputs into one output, like plugging in trees of operations.
18M.entry: Count the ways to bracket a times b times c times d (5 ways). Draw each as a tree and see how trees plug into trees, the idea of an operad.

18N.idea: Higher categories have arrows between arrows between arrows, used to treat 'the same up to deformation' precisely.
18N.entry: Two paths across a field from A to B: if you can slide one into the other without crossing a pond, the slide is an arrow between arrows. Find two paths with no slide.

19A.idea: K-theory starts by turning things you can add but not subtract, like piles of objects, into a group with negatives.
19A.entry: Build integers from pairs of natural numbers: (5,3) means 5 minus 3. Decide when two pairs are the same, the trick Grothendieck used for K0.

19B.idea: K1 asks which invertible matrices can be reduced to simple ones by row operations, measuring what is left over.
19B.entry: Using only 'add a multiple of one row to another', try to turn a 2x2 matrix into the identity. Show you can exactly when its determinant is 1.

19C.idea: K2 records the hidden relations among elementary row operations, the ways they cancel unexpectedly.
19C.entry: Best glimpse: on a 2x2 grid, 'add row 1 to row 2' then 'subtract row 2 from row 1' and so on; find a sequence of such moves that returns to the start.

19D.idea: Higher algebraic K-theory builds an infinite ladder of invariants of rings using topology.
19D.entry: Honest glimpse only: K-groups of the integers are linked to Bernoulli numbers. Compute sums of powers 1+2+...+n and 1^2+...+n^2 to meet those numbers.

19E.idea: K-theory in geometry counts ways to lay bundles of directions over a shape, giving invariants of spaces.
19E.entry: Make a paper strip into a cylinder and a Mobius band; draw arrows across the strip. One band lets arrows flip direction going around. These are two different line bundles.

19F.idea: K-theory in number theory links algebraic invariants to deep facts about primes and values of zeta functions.
19F.entry: Honest glimpse: check that 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + ... approaches pi squared over 6 by adding terms on a calculator; K-theory explains patterns in such values.

19G.idea: K-theory of forms classifies quadratic forms, like sums of squares, up to change of variables, using group addition.
19G.entry: Which numbers are sums of two squares? Test 1 to 50. Then check that the product of two such sums is again one, so sums of squares can be combined.

19J.idea: Obstructions from topology use K-theory to decide whether a shape can be simplified or built from finitely many pieces.
19J.entry: Best glimpse: can you untangle this loop of string into a circle? Some knots refuse; an invariant (like counting colourings of the diagram) proves the obstruction exists.

19K.idea: K-theory of operator algebras counts infinite-dimensional pieces like projections, linking analysis to topology.
19K.entry: Hilbert's hotel: shift every guest up one room. Shifting is undoable one way but not the other, and the one missing room is the index, a K-theory number.

19L.idea: Topological K-theory classifies vector bundles on spaces, and gives famous results like which spheres admit independent direction fields.
19L.entry: Hairy ball: try to comb a fuzzy tennis ball flat with no crown. You cannot, yet on a donut you can. K-theory tells exactly when such combing works.

19M.idea: Miscellaneous applications of K-theory, from physics of materials to index theorems, use it to count robust features.
19M.entry: Count how many times a wiggly loop drawn around a point winds around it; small wiggles do not change the count, the kind of robust number K-theory produces.

20A.idea: A group is a set of moves you can combine and undo, and the axioms capture exactly what symmetry needs.
20A.entry: List the symmetries of a square (4 turns, 4 flips). Fill in the 8x8 table of 'do this then that' using a cut-out paper square.

20B.idea: Permutation groups study shuffles of a set, and which arrangements can be reached by given moves.
20B.entry: The 15 puzzle: show, by counting swaps, that switching just the 14 and 15 tiles is impossible. Sam Loyd's prize was safe.

20C.idea: Representation theory turns abstract symmetries into matrices or number patterns, making groups computable.
20C.entry: Rotations of a square as 2x2 grids of 0, 1, -1: write each and multiply them to check they follow the same table as the turns themselves.

20D.idea: Finite groups can be broken into simple building blocks, like primes for numbers, and the simple ones are fully classified.
20D.entry: Find all ways to arrange 6 symmetries: compare turns of a hexagon with symmetries of a triangle. One commutes, one does not, so two different groups of size 6.

20E.idea: Infinite and finite groups are classified by how they are assembled from smaller pieces and what they act on.
20E.entry: Wallpaper patterns: hunt for rotations and mirrors in floor tiles. There are only 17 types of wallpaper symmetry; sort a few patterns into their types.

20F.idea: Groups given by generators and rules can be studied by their geometry, like the street maps of the moves.
20F.entry: Draw the map of moves for 'a' and 'b' where ab equals ba: you get a grid. Where nothing commutes you get an ever-branching tree. Compare how fast they grow.

20G.idea: Linear algebraic groups are symmetry groups defined by polynomial equations, like rotations or invertible matrices.
20G.entry: Count invertible 2x2 matrices with entries 0 or 1 under arithmetic mod 2 (there are 6). Check they shuffle the three nonzero vectors in all 6 ways.

20H.idea: Groups of matrices, such as those with integer entries, act on the plane or space and generate beautiful patterns.
20H.entry: Apply the matrices [[1,1],[0,1]] and [[1,0],[1,1]] repeatedly to (1,1). Every pair of coprime whole numbers appears, linking to fractions in the Stern-Brocot tree.

20J.idea: Homological tools measure how groups fit together, for example whether a big group splits into simpler parts.
20J.entry: Clock mod 4 contains mod 2 as the even hours, with mod 2 left over. Yet it is not two mod-2 clocks side by side. Find the element that shows why.

20K.idea: Abelian groups, where order never matters, are completely described by lists of clock sizes.
20K.entry: Show that mod-6 arithmetic is the same as a mod-2 clock and a mod-3 clock running together, but mod 4 is not two mod-2 clocks.

20L.idea: Groupoids are like groups but with moves only allowed from certain states, keeping track of where you are.
20L.entry: Fifteen puzzle states as dots, legal slides as two-way arrows. Each move is undoable, but only joinable when it starts where the last ended: a groupoid, not a group.

20M.idea: Semigroups are moves you can combine but not necessarily undo, modelling processes that forget information.
20M.entry: Functions on {1,2,3}: 'send everything to 1' cannot be undone. Combine a few such functions and find which combinations are still reversible.

20N.idea: Loops and quasigroups relax group rules, keeping the ability to solve equations but not associativity.
20N.entry: A completed Sudoku row-column table (a Latin square) is a quasigroup's multiplication table. Fill a 4x4 Latin square and test whether (ab)c equals a(bc).

20P.idea: Random methods answer questions about groups, like the chance that two random symmetries commute or how fast shuffles mix.
20P.entry: Pick two random symmetries of a triangle; what is the chance they commute? (1/2.) Then ask how many riffle shuffles mix a deck: about seven.

22A.idea: Some number systems let you both combine things and move smoothly between them, so algebra and nearness live together.
22A.entry: Turn a clock hand: rotations add like numbers, and a tiny turn is close to no turn. Compare with a 12-hour clock where you can only jump.

22B.idea: Repeating patterns, like sound waves, can be built from pure tones, and the same idea works on circles, lines and clocks.
22B.entry: Add the columns of a 4-hour clock table using 'secret codes' 1, i, -1, -i, and see a lopsided list of numbers split into four pure rhythms.

22C.idea: Groups that are finite in size but smooth, like all rotations of a sphere, can be averaged over fairly.
22C.entry: Average a doodle over all 4 quarter-turns of a square to make it symmetric; then imagine averaging over every angle of a circle.

22D.idea: Big symmetry groups can be studied by how they act as matrices or on functions, turning shape into algebra.
22D.entry: Write the 6 symmetries of a triangle as ways to shuffle three corners, then as 2-by-2 rotation and flip pictures, and check both multiply the same way.

22E.idea: Smooth symmetries, like all rotations, are understood from their tiny infinitesimal nudges.
22E.entry: Turn a book 90 degrees forward then 90 sideways, then undo in the other order: it ends up tilted. Small turns almost commute, big ones do not.

22F.idea: Infinite symmetry groups, like all translations and stretches, push points around a space forever without coming back.
22F.entry: Mark a dot on graph paper and apply 'double x, halve y' over and over: the dot slides along a hyperbola and never returns. Which curves are left unchanged?

26A.idea: How a single real function behaves: is it continuous, does it have a slope, can we add up its area?
26A.entry: Draw a staircase and a ramp between the same points. Which can you draw without lifting your pencil? Which has a slope everywhere? Zoom in on corners.

26B.idea: Functions with several inputs, like height on a hill map, have slopes in every direction and volumes underneath.
26B.entry: On a contour map, find the steepest way up from a dot: it always crosses contour lines at right angles. Check with a ruler.

26C.idea: Polynomials have hidden rules about where they cross zero and how many times they can wiggle.
26C.entry: Descartes' rule of signs: count sign changes in x^3 - 2x^2 - x + 2 and guess how many positive roots; then find them by trying 1, 2, -1.

26D.idea: Inequalities compare quantities without computing them, like the fact that an average of numbers is at least their geometric mean.
26D.entry: Of all rectangles with perimeter 20, which has the biggest area? Try 1x9, 2x8, 5x5, then see why (a+b)/2 is at least sqrt(ab).

26E.idea: A grab bag of unusual ways to do calculus: infinitesimals, fuzzy values, set-valued functions, and different kinds of averages.
26E.entry: Compare four averages of 2 and 8: arithmetic 5, geometric 4, harmonic 3.2, and root-mean-square. Which fits average speed on a round trip?

28A.idea: Measure theory gives a careful meaning to length, area and probability, even for very ragged sets.
28A.entry: Remove the middle third of a line segment, then the middle thirds of what is left, forever. Total removed is 1, yet uncountably many points remain.

28B.idea: Measures and integrals can produce vectors or other objects instead of plain numbers.
28B.entry: Spread mass along a bent wire and add up mass times position as arrows: the result is the balance point, a vector-valued 'integral'.

28C.idea: On spaces with symmetry, there is a natural fair way to measure size that every symmetry respects.
28C.entry: Why is 'pick a random angle' fair but 'pick a random slope' not? Throw darts at a circle and compare angle and slope histograms.

28D.idea: If a system keeps mixing for long enough, averaging over time gives the same answer as averaging over all states.
28D.entry: Keep multiplying by 2 and keeping the fractional part, starting at 0.1234. Tally which tenth each value lands in: the time average matches the space average.

28E.idea: Odd corners of measure theory: infinitesimal measures, fuzzy measures, and sets so strange they cannot be measured at all.
28E.entry: Vitali's puzzle in words: sort numbers in [0,1) into piles that differ by a rational. Pick one from each pile. Why can that set have no sensible length?

30A.idea: Complex functions, which turn points of a plane into points of a plane, are amazingly rigid once they are smooth.
30A.entry: Square each point on a grid of complex numbers and plot the results: right angles between grid lines stay right angles everywhere except at 0.

30B.idea: A smooth complex function equals an infinite power series, and the series works out to the nearest trouble spot.
30B.entry: Add 1 - x^2 + x^4 - ... for x = 0.5 and x = 1.5. It fits 1/(1+x^2) only for |x|<1, because of hidden trouble at x = i.

30C.idea: Complex functions bend regions of the plane while keeping angles, and any simple blob can be bent into a disc.
30C.entry: Draw a grid on a balloon, then squash it: small squares turn into small squares of new sizes. Check with z -> z^2 on graph paper.

30D.idea: Functions smooth on the whole complex plane, like e^z, are tied by how fast they grow to how many zeros they have.
30D.entry: A polynomial of degree n has n roots and grows like |z|^n. Plot |z^3 - 1| along big circles and count roughly how the growth gives three roots.

30E.idea: Puzzles of fitting and approximating functions in the complex plane, like how well polynomials can mimic given shapes.
30E.entry: Find the straight line through 3 given points that misses by the least worst-case amount; this is the simplest version of best approximation.

30F.idea: Some functions, like square root, are many-valued, and become single-valued on a cleverly glued multi-sheeted surface.
30F.entry: Walk once around 0 tracking sqrt(z) with a pencil: you come back with the opposite sign. Make a two-sheet paper model with a slit glued crosswise.

30G.idea: The rules of complex functions can be copied to new settings, like grids, quaternions or p-adic numbers.
30G.entry: Discrete analytic functions: fill a grid so each square's diagonal differences match (a-c = i(b-d)). Check that z works and z^2 nearly does.

30H.idea: Families of nice functions on a disc can be treated like vector spaces with sizes and distances.
30H.entry: Treat polynomials as vectors: add them, scale them, and measure their size as the largest value on a circle. Is |p+q| at most |p|+|q|?

30J.idea: Functions on the unit disc are controlled by their boundary values and by how they shrink the disc.
30J.entry: Schwarz lemma glimpse: if a map keeps the disc inside itself and 0 at 0, it can't stretch anything. Try z -> z^2 and z/2 on points.

30K.idea: One single function can, by shifting or zooming, approximate every possible function: a universal pattern hiding everything.
30K.entry: The digits 0.123456789101112... (Champernowne) contain every finite digit string, including your birthday. Find it. Universal functions do the same for shapes.

30L.idea: Calculus ideas like slope and stretch can be done on spaces with only distances, no coordinates.
30L.entry: On a taxicab grid, measure distances and find all points equidistant from two corners. Shapes change but ideas like 'midpoint' still make sense.

31A.idea: Harmonic functions, like steady temperature on a plate, always equal the average of their neighbours.
31A.entry: Fill a grid with fixed edge numbers, then repeatedly replace each inside cell by the average of its 4 neighbours. It settles to a smooth steady state.

31B.idea: The same averaging rule in 3D describes gravity, electricity and steady heat, with no hills or pits inside.
31B.entry: Why is there no gravity inside a hollow ball? Compare pulls from near and far patches of shell using area ~ distance squared.

31C.idea: Averaging and potentials extend to graphs, random walks and other settings beyond flat space.
31C.entry: On a path of 5 squares, a random walker stops at either end. The win chance from each square is the average of its neighbours: 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1.

31D.idea: Potential theory boiled down to a few axioms about averaging, so it applies to many different equations at once.
31D.entry: List three rules a 'smooth out' operation must follow (no new peaks, averaging, stability), then test them on grid averaging and on random walks.

31E.idea: Heat flow and averaging can be done on fractals like the Sierpinski triangle, giving strange new dimensions.
31E.entry: Random walk on the Sierpinski gasket graph: count steps to cross level 1, 2, 3. Each level multiplies time by 5, not 4, so walks are slow.

32A.idea: Functions of several complex variables behave very differently from one variable: for example, holes can force themselves to fill in.
32A.entry: Hard to show directly. Glimpse: in one variable 1/z blows up at a point; in two variables, try to make a function blow up only at a single point and fail.

32B.idea: Near a point, solution sets of complex equations look like a few simple pieces glued together.
32B.entry: Plot real solutions of y^2 = x^2 and y^2 = x^3 near the origin: a cross and a cusp. Zoom in: these are the local shapes.

32C.idea: Shapes cut out by complex equations, including singular ones, can be studied like smooth surfaces with care.
32C.entry: Sketch y^2 = x^2(x+1): a loop with a self-crossing. Discuss how a spaceship moving along it could pass through the crossing twice.

32D.idea: How far a smooth complex function can be extended; in several variables, functions often extend automatically into holes.
32D.entry: Analytic continuation in one variable: 1+x+x^2+... = 1/(1-x) lets you 'extend' the sum's meaning to x = 2, giving -1. Debate whether that is fair.

32E.idea: Which regions of complex space are natural homes for functions, judged by a special kind of convexity.
32E.entry: Warm-up with real convexity: test shapes by checking whether every segment between two points stays inside. Then note complex space uses a twisted version.

32F.idea: Convexity in several complex variables uses complex lines and curves instead of straight segments.
32F.entry: Real convexity on paper: which of these shapes is convex? A star, a disc, a crescent. The complex version is the same game with curved test lines.

32G.idea: Complex shapes can be continuously wiggled into each other, and we study all possible wiggles at once.
32G.entry: A flat torus from a parallelogram: slide one corner and the donut changes shape. Which slides give the same donut? Tile the plane to check.

32H.idea: Maps between regions of complex space are very rigid: there are far fewer than you would expect.
32H.entry: Glimpse: in one variable a disc can be mapped onto any simple blob, but in two variables a ball and a 'polydisc' cannot be matched. Only words reach this.

32J.idea: Closed complex shapes with no edges, like the torus, carry very few global functions.
32J.entry: A function on a donut made by gluing a square's edges must repeat both ways. Try to draw a smooth repeating height map with no highest point: impossible.

32K.idea: Extensions of complex analytic spaces to infinite dimensions and other more general settings.
32K.entry: Honestly very hard. Glimpse: a polynomial in infinitely many variables x1 + x2^2/2 + x3^3/3 + ...; when does it add up to a finite number?

32L.idea: Complex spaces can carry a family of attached spaces, like a fibre at every point, twisting globally.
32L.entry: Make a Möbius strip: a line attached at every point of a circle with a twist. Cut it down the middle and see why the twist can't be undone.

32M.idea: Complex shapes with lots of symmetry, where a group moves every point to every other.
32M.entry: The disc's symmetries: rotations and maps that slide any point to the centre. Draw circles through a point and see how they move.

32N.idea: Functions of several complex variables that repeat under a large symmetry group, generalizing wallpaper patterns.
32N.entry: Start with a wallpaper pattern that repeats in two directions; then imagine repeats in four real directions at once. Only a glimpse is possible.

32P.idea: Doing analysis with p-adic numbers, where closeness means divisible by a high power of p.
32P.entry: In 10-adic land 1, 11, 111, 1111... home in on a number. Show ...9999 + 1 = 0, so ...9999 behaves like -1.

32Q.idea: Smooth shapes that look locally like complex space, with extra geometry like curvature.
32Q.entry: The Riemann sphere: put a ball on the plane and project from the north pole. Every point of the plane, plus one 'infinity', gets a spot.

32S.idea: Points where complex curves pinch or cross, and how small loops around them knot together.
32S.entry: Draw y^2 = x^3 and zoom on the cusp. Then a teaser: around the cusp in complex space, the curve meets a small sphere in a trefoil knot.

32T.idea: Regions in complex space shaped well enough that every reasonable equation can be solved on them.
32T.entry: Honestly very hard. Glimpse via real convexity: on a convex region, a straight path from any point to any other stays inside, so problems spread nicely.

32U.idea: Potential theory in several complex variables, using functions that are below average on every complex line.
32U.entry: Take log of distance to the origin on a grid and test the averaging rule around circles. Pluripotential theory asks this on every complex slice.

32V.idea: Boundaries of complex regions carry their own leftover complex structure, a mix of real and complex directions.
32V.entry: Very hard. Glimpse: the 3-sphere in two complex variables has, at each point, one 'real only' direction and one complex plane. Use a picture of Hopf circles.

32W.idea: Special differential equations in several complex variables, especially the one that tests whether a function is complex-smooth.
32W.entry: Check the Cauchy-Riemann test: for f = x^2 - y^2 + i(2xy), compare slopes in x and y; for x^2 + y^2 it fails.

33B.idea: Exponentials, logarithms, trig functions and the gamma function are the basic building blocks used everywhere.
33B.entry: Fill in 1, 1, 2, 6, 24, ... (factorials) and ask what 'half factorial' should be. Plot points and guess; the answer is sqrt(pi)/2.

33C.idea: Hypergeometric series are a single family that includes most famous functions as special cases.
33C.entry: Ratios of consecutive terms: for 1+x+x^2+... the ratio is x; for e^x it is x/(n+1). Any series with a nice ratio rule is hypergeometric.

33D.idea: Basic hypergeometric series are q-versions of classical functions, linked to counting partitions.
33D.entry: Count ways to write 5 as sums of positive whole numbers (7 ways). Then expand (1+q)(1+q^2)(1+q^3)... and read off partitions into distinct parts.

33E.idea: Other named functions, like Bessel-type, elliptic and Lambert W, that arise from specific problems.
33E.entry: Solve x * 2^x = 8 by trial: x = 2. Now try x * 2^x = 10. No algebra works, so the Lambert W function is named to answer it.

33F.idea: How to compute special functions fast and accurately on a computer.
33F.entry: Compute e by adding 1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/6 + ... and count how many terms give 6 correct digits. Compare with (1+1/n)^n.

34A.idea: A differential equation describes how something changes, and its solution traces out the whole future from a starting point.
34A.entry: Population doubles each year when growth is proportional to size. Draw a slope field for y' = y and sketch curves from different starting heights.

34B.idea: Sometimes we know conditions at both ends, not just the start, which can give no solution, one, or many.
34B.entry: Throw a ball to land exactly at a target: adjust launch speed by trial and error (the shooting method). Some targets have two arcs, high and low.

34C.idea: We can describe the long-run shape of solutions, like cycles and spirals, without solving the equation.
34C.entry: Rabbits and foxes: rabbits up means foxes rise, then rabbits fall, then foxes fall. Sketch a loop in a rabbits-versus-foxes picture.

34D.idea: Stability asks whether a small push dies away or grows, like a marble in a bowl versus on a hilltop.
34D.entry: Balance a pencil on its tip versus hang it from a string. Then iterate 'y -> y/2' and 'y -> 2y' from 0.01 and watch.

34E.idea: Approximate solutions when some quantity is very large or very small, often revealing thin layers of fast change.
34E.entry: Cooling coffee with a tiny parameter: a fast drop at first, then slow drift. Sketch two zoom levels of the same curve and match them.

34F.idea: Differential equations with random kicks, such as a population shaken by luck each year.
34F.entry: Simulate savings growing 5 percent a year plus a coin flip of +10 or -10. Run several players and compare spread with the smooth curve.

34G.idea: Differential equations whose unknowns are themselves whole functions or infinite lists.
34G.entry: A row of 10 cups passing water to neighbours each minute: write one change rule for the whole list. Imagine infinitely many cups.

34H.idea: Control theory: choosing inputs to steer a changing system where you want it.
34H.entry: Park a toy car: you can only go forward/back and steer. Show you can still move sideways by wiggling, like parallel parking.

34K.idea: Equations where the rate of change depends on the past, like a delay, which can cause oscillations.
34K.entry: Shower temperature with a 5-second delay: adjust based on what you feel now and overshoot back and forth. Simulate with a table.

34L.idea: Differential equations viewed as operators with special 'eigen' solutions, like the notes of a vibrating string.
34L.entry: Pluck a string held at both ends: only waves that fit a whole number of half-wavelengths survive. Draw the first three and find their pitches.

34M.idea: Differential equations with complex numbers, where going around a singular point can change the solution.
34M.entry: Follow sqrt(z), a solution of 2zy' = y, once around 0: you return with a minus sign. The equation remembers the loop.

34N.idea: A single theory covering both smooth change and step-by-step change, and mixtures of the two.
34N.entry: Compare money growing 10 percent a year in one jump with continuous growth, then a calendar with jumps on weekdays and smooth weekends.

35A.idea: A PDE links how a quantity changes in several directions at once; the first question is whether a solution exists and is unique.
35A.entry: On a grid, each cell must equal the average of its four neighbours, with the border numbers fixed. Fill in a 3x3 interior by trial and see there is exactly one answer.

35B.idea: Without solving a PDE you can still prove things about solutions, like where the biggest value must sit or how fast things settle.
35B.entry: On a grid where each inside cell is the average of its neighbours, argue the largest number must lie on the border. Try to break this and fail.

35C.idea: Some PDE solutions can be written as explicit formulas, such as travelling waves, sums of simple waves, or similarity shapes.
35C.entry: A wave on a rope keeps its shape and slides along: plot y=f(x-t) for a bump at t=0,1,2 and see it move right at speed 1.

35D.idea: Real solutions can have corners and jumps, so mathematicians widen what counts as a solution to include these rough shapes.
35D.entry: Cars in a traffic jam: draw the speed along a road where fast cars meet a queue. The sharp jump is a shock that no smooth formula describes.

35E.idea: When the rules of a PDE do not change from place to place, waves of the form sine and exponential turn it into plain algebra.
35E.entry: Guess y=e^(kx) in y''=4y and get k^2=4. The derivative rule becomes a number equation; repeat with sines for y''=-9y.

35F.idea: First-order PDEs carry information along lines, called characteristics, so you can solve them by following each line.
35F.entry: A conveyor belt carries sand piles at constant speed. Mark where a pile at x=2 is after 3 seconds; the pile shape just rides along each line x-vt.

35G.idea: Higher-order PDEs, like the bending of a plate or beam, involve fourth derivatives and need more boundary conditions.
35G.entry: Clamp a ruler at one end and push the tip: it curves smoothly. Compare with a string, which can bend sharply. Stiffness means higher derivatives.

35H.idea: Some equations smooth out rough data even though they only push in certain directions, as long as those directions combine to reach everywhere.
35H.entry: Parallel parking: you can only drive forward/back or turn, yet wiggling lets you slide sideways. Moves that combine to reach every direction are the key idea.

35J.idea: Elliptic equations describe balanced, steady states, like a soap film or heated plate at rest, where each point equals the average around it.
35J.entry: Bend a wire loop and dip it in soap: the film is the smoothest surface. On paper, relax a grid where each cell becomes the average of its neighbours.

35K.idea: Parabolic equations describe spreading and smoothing over time, like heat flowing or ink diffusing, with sharp features fading fast.
35K.entry: Row of numbers 0,0,100,0,0: each step replace each by the average of itself and neighbours. Watch the spike spread and flatten, and the total stay fixed.

35L.idea: Hyperbolic equations describe waves that travel at finite speed and keep their sharpness, like sound, light, or a plucked string.
35L.entry: Two people shake a long rope from opposite ends. The pulses pass through each other unchanged. Sketch them before, during and after meeting.

35M.idea: Some equations behave like waves in one region and like steady balance in another, as in air flowing past a plane near the sound barrier.
35M.entry: A boat moving slower than ripples sends waves ahead; faster than ripples it leaves a V wake. Measure the V angle in a photo and relate to speed.

35N.idea: Some problems impose more conditions than needed, so solutions exist only for special shapes; a classic answer is that the shape must be a ball.
35N.entry: Which shapes of a frying pan cook evenly so the edge always gets the same heat flow? Argue a circle works by symmetry and a square cannot.

35P.idea: A drum or string can only vibrate at special frequencies set by its shape, and studying these notes reveals the shape's geometry.
35P.entry: Tap glasses filled with different water levels or press a guitar string at half and a third its length: notes at 2x and 3x the base frequency.

35Q.idea: PDEs are the language of physics, from fluids and heat to quantum particles and finance, each with its own famous equation.
35Q.entry: Drop food colouring into still water versus stirred water. Describe in words what the heat equation and the fluid equation must each say.

35R.idea: Odd PDE settings: shapes with moving boundaries, unknown insides found from outside measurements, random noise, or equations on networks.
35R.entry: Melting ice cube: the boundary between ice and water moves. Measure an ice cube each 5 minutes and plot how the edge recedes.

35S.idea: Pseudodifferential operators treat a derivative as multiplication by frequency, so you can define half a derivative or any frequency filter.
35S.entry: Hard to make elementary. Glimpse: if differentiating sin(kx) multiplies its wiggle size by k, what operation would multiply it by the square root of k?

37A.idea: Ergodic theory asks whether one long journey visits every region in fair proportion, so time averages equal space averages.
37A.entry: Keep adding 0.618 and keep only the fractional part. Tally how many land in each tenth from 0 to 1 after 50 steps. Every bin fills evenly.

37B.idea: Topological dynamics studies repeated maps through what returns, what mixes, and what stays fixed, ignoring exact distances.
37B.entry: Shuffle a deck with perfect riffle shuffles: after 8 shuffles it returns to the start. Try with 10 cards and find the return time.

37C.idea: Smooth dynamical systems follow points moving under a smooth rule, looking for fixed points, cycles and how nearby paths behave.
37C.entry: Press cos repeatedly on a calculator in radians. Any start converges to 0.739. Draw the cobweb diagram showing why it is attracting.

37D.idea: In hyperbolic systems nearby points separate exponentially in some directions while being squeezed in others, causing chaos that is still structured.
37D.entry: Baker's map: stretch a square of dough to double width, cut, stack. Track two raisins that start close; after a few folds they are far apart.

37E.idea: In one or two dimensions, simple maps already show period doubling and chaos, and order follows strict rules like period three implies chaos.
37E.entry: Iterate x to 3.2x(1-x), then 3.5x(1-x), then 3.9x(1-x) on a calculator. See a 2-cycle, a 4-cycle, then no pattern.

37F.idea: Iterating maps like z to z^2+c on complex numbers creates the Julia and Mandelbrot sets, whose boundaries are fractal.
37F.entry: With c=-1, iterate z to z^2+c from 0 and from 1. With c=1 it blows up. Test real c values and shade those that stay bounded.

37G.idea: Bifurcation theory studies how the long-run behaviour of a system suddenly changes as a dial is slowly turned.
37G.entry: Slowly tilt a book with a coin on it: nothing, nothing, then it slides. Or bend a ruler by squeezing its ends until it snaps sideways.

37H.idea: Random dynamical systems apply a randomly chosen rule each step, and can still settle into predictable patterns.
37H.entry: Chaos game: pick a triangle's corner by die roll and move halfway there, repeat 50 times. The dots draw a Sierpinski triangle.

37J.idea: Hamiltonian systems conserve energy and phase-space area, which forbids attractors and gives regular orbits mixed with chaos.
37J.entry: A pendulum swings forever without friction. Plot angle against speed for several energies: nested loops, never spiralling in.

37K.idea: Some wave equations have infinitely many conserved quantities, giving solitary waves that pass through each other unchanged.
37K.entry: Solitons: a single wave travelled miles along a Scottish canal in 1834. Simulate with a row of balls on springs or recall Newton's cradle.

37L.idea: Systems with friction in infinitely many dimensions, like turbulent fluids, often settle onto a finite-dimensional attractor.
37L.entry: Stir a cup of tea and watch: the swirl fades to a few slow eddies. Count how many big eddies remain after 10 seconds.

37M.idea: Computers simulate dynamics in tiny steps, and the choice of method decides whether errors stay small or blow up.
37M.entry: Simulate a ball orbiting with Euler steps on graph paper. The orbit spirals outward. Then update speed first and position second, and it stays closed.

37N.idea: Dynamical systems model populations, epidemics, economies and planets, revealing cycles, tipping points and chaos in the real world.
37N.entry: Rabbits and foxes: start 100 rabbits, 10 foxes, with simple yearly rules. Tabulate 10 years and see the boom and bust cycle.

37P.idea: Iterate maps on whole numbers, fractions or numbers mod p, and ask which starts cycle and how long cycles are.
37P.entry: Iterate x to x^2+1 mod 11 from 0. List values until one repeats, giving a rho shape. This is how Pollard factors numbers.

39A.idea: Difference equations give each term from earlier terms, the discrete cousin of differential equations.
39A.entry: Fibonacci rabbits: each term is the sum of the previous two. Compute ratios of terms and watch them settle near 1.618.

39B.idea: A functional equation describes a function only by a rule it obeys, like f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y), and asks what functions fit.
39B.entry: Find all f with f(x+y)=f(x)f(y) and f(1)=2. Work out f(2), f(3), f(0), f(-1), f(1/2) and spot powers of 2.

40A.idea: An infinite process may settle to a limit or not, and tests tell which, sometimes with surprising answers.
40A.entry: Harmonic series: group 1/3+1/4, then 1/5 to 1/8 and so on. Each group exceeds 1/2, so the sum grows forever, though slowly.

40B.idea: With double sequences and series, the order in which you add rows and columns can change the answer.
40B.entry: Grid with 1s on the diagonal and -1s just right of it. Sum rows first: 0. Sum columns first: 1. Find why the order matters.

40C.idea: Summability methods assign sensible values to divergent series, for example by averaging partial sums.
40C.entry: Grandi's series 1-1+1-1... has partial sums 1,0,1,0. Average them: 1, 1/2, 2/3, 1/2, 3/5... The averages approach 1/2.

40D.idea: Abelian theorems say a good averaging method gives the true sum whenever the series already converges.
40D.entry: Partial sums approach 3. Show that running averages of the partial sums also approach 3. Test with sums 2.5, 2.9, 2.99, 2.999.

40E.idea: Tauberian theorems run the other way: if the average converges and the terms are not too wild, the series itself converges.
40E.entry: Partial sums 1,0,1,0 average to 1/2 but do not converge, because the terms stay size 1. Find a series whose shrinking terms fix that.

40F.idea: Absolute summability asks that the averaged sums settle firmly enough that their total wobble is finite, not just eventually small.
40F.entry: Compare 1-1/2+1/3-1/4... with the same signs all positive. One converges, one does not. Rearrange the first to approach 2 instead.

40G.idea: Special methods like Abel, Borel and Euler summation each tame divergent series in their own way, sometimes giving the same value.
40G.entry: Abel's trick: 1-x+x^2-x^3... equals 1/(1+x). Put x=0.9, 0.99, 0.999 and see the answer approach 1/2 for 1-1+1-1...

40H.idea: Summation methods can be seen as infinite matrices acting on sequences, and functional analysis tells which ones are reliable.
40H.entry: Write the averaging rule as a triangle of numbers: row n has n entries 1/n. Apply rows to 1,0,1,0,... to get the averaged sequence.

40J.idea: Summability ideas extend to sequences of vectors, functions, or elements of groups and other abstract settings.
40J.entry: Hard to make concrete. Glimpse: average the positions of a point hopping around a square's corners; the average heads to the centre.

41A.idea: Approximation theory asks how well simple functions like polynomials can mimic complicated ones and how fast the error shrinks.
41A.entry: Approximate sin(0.5) with x, then x-x^3/6, then add x^5/120. Compare to the calculator and count correct digits each time.

42A.idea: Any periodic signal can be built by adding sine waves of different frequencies, and the recipe of amounts tells you its sound.
42A.entry: Add sin x + sin(3x)/3 + sin(5x)/5 at a few points and plot. A square wave appears, with little overshoots at the jumps.

42B.idea: Fourier ideas in several dimensions break pictures into stripe patterns, which explains image compression and blurring.
42B.entry: Look through a fine mesh curtain at another mesh: moire stripes appear. Draw two sets of slightly tilted lines and see the big wave.

42C.idea: Signals can be built from building blocks other than sines, such as wavelets or Walsh square waves, each suited to different jobs.
42C.entry: Haar wavelet: take 8 numbers, replace pairs by average and half-difference, repeat. Zero the small differences and rebuild a close copy.

43A.idea: Fourier analysis works on any symmetry group, splitting functions into pieces that behave simply under the group's moves.
43A.entry: Clock arithmetic mod 4: split the pattern 3,1,4,1 into constant, alternating and rotating parts by adding with signs +1,-1,+i,-i.

44A.idea: Integral transforms turn hard problems such as differential equations into easier algebra, then transform back.
44A.entry: Logarithms as a transform: multiply 23x47 by adding logs and taking back. Laplace transforms do the same for calculus.

45A.idea: In a linear integral equation the unknown function appears inside an integral, adding up its values weighted by a kernel.
45A.entry: Savings: today's balance is starting money plus the sum of past balances times interest. Write it as a running sum and solve by steps.

45B.idea: Fredholm equations integrate over a fixed range, and like matrix systems they either have one solution or a special resonance.
45B.entry: Chop the interval into 3 points: the integral becomes a 3x3 matrix equation. Solve it and note when the matrix is singular.

45C.idea: Eigenvalue problems for integral equations find special functions that the integral just rescales, like natural modes.
45C.entry: Matrix version: find a vector that a 2x2 averaging matrix only stretches. Try (1,1) and (1,-1) for [[0.7,0.3],[0.3,0.7]].

45D.idea: Volterra equations integrate only over the past, so the solution is built step by step forward in time.
45D.entry: Population where births depend on everyone born in the last 3 years. Tabulate year by year from 10 founders and see growth.

45E.idea: Singular integral equations have kernels that blow up, like 1/(x-y), yet still give meaning and model cracks and airfoils.
45E.entry: Hard to make faithful. Glimpse: sum 1/(x-k) over k from -10 to 10, skipping k=x; nearby terms cancel in pairs though each is huge.

45F.idea: Systems of integral equations couple several unknown functions whose histories feed into each other.
45F.entry: Two bank accounts each earning interest on the other's past balance. Tabulate both year by year and watch them grow together.

45G.idea: Nonlinear integral equations have the unknown inside the integral in a nonlinear way, giving multiple or no solutions.
45G.entry: Rumour spread: new hearers today depend on past hearers times those not yet told. Tabulate a town of 100 and watch an S curve.

45H.idea: Integral equations with special kernels, such as differences of arguments, can be solved by tricks like Fourier or convolution.
45H.entry: Convolution: blurring a row of pixels by averaging with neighbours. Given the blurred row 1,2,3,2,1, try to recover the original.

45J.idea: Integro-differential equations combine rates of change with memory of the whole past, as in materials that remember stress.
45J.entry: Memory foam: press a hand in and let go; the dent fills slowly. Time it and plot depth versus seconds.

45K.idea: Integro-PDEs mix spatial change with long-range or past-dependent effects, like animals that jump far as well as wander.
45K.entry: Seeds spread by wind: most land nearby, some far. On a line of cells, move each seed by dice and compare with neighbour-only steps.

45L.idea: When integral equations cannot be solved exactly, you approximate by sums over grid points and check the error shrinks.
45L.entry: Estimate the area under y=x^2 from 0 to 1 with 4 and then 8 rectangles. Watch the error halve each time.

45M.idea: We study how solutions of integral equations behave in the long run: growth, decay, stability or oscillation.
45M.entry: In the birth-memory population model, change the birth rate and see when the population dies out versus grows.

45N.idea: Integral equations can be posed for functions taking values in abstract spaces, using operator theory instead of formulas.
45N.entry: Hard to make elementary. Glimpse: solve x = 1 + 0.5x by repeating x to 1+0.5x from 0; the same repetition works for functions.

45P.idea: Integral operators turn one function into another by weighted averaging, and their size and smoothing power are the main questions.
45P.entry: Running average of 7 days smooths a jumpy temperature list. Apply it twice and see the result is smoother still.

45Q.idea: Inverse problems recover a hidden cause from smeared measurements, often unstable so small errors are greatly amplified.
45Q.entry: CT scan puzzle: a 3x3 grid of hidden numbers with known row, column and diagonal sums. Reconstruct the grid.

45R.idea: Random integral equations have noisy kernels or inputs, and ask how randomness in the memory affects the answer.
45R.entry: Savings with dice interest: each year roll to set the rate. Simulate a few accounts and compare their spread over 10 years.

46A.idea: Spaces where you can add things and scale them, and also say when things are getting close, even with infinitely many directions.
46A.entry: Treat infinite lists of numbers as points. Is (1,1/2,1/3,...) 'close' to all zeros? Try three different ways to measure the gap and see they disagree.

46B.idea: A norm is a way to measure the size of a vector; different norms give different shapes for the 'unit ball'.
46B.entry: On grid paper draw all points at distance 1 from the origin using taxi distance, ordinary distance and 'biggest coordinate' distance: a diamond, a circle, a square.

46C.idea: Hilbert spaces carry angles and lengths into infinitely many dimensions, so Pythagoras and projection still work.
46C.entry: Add 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + ... as the squared length of the infinite arrow (1, 1/2, 1/3, ...). Pythagoras in infinitely many dimensions gives a finite length.

46E.idea: Whole collections of functions can be treated as spaces, and we can measure how far apart two functions are.
46E.entry: Draw y=x and y=x² on [0,1]. Measure their distance as the biggest vertical gap, then as the area between them. Which pairs of functions are closest?

46F.idea: Some useful objects, like a perfect instant kick or point mass, are not functions but can be handled by how they act when averaged.
46F.entry: Make narrower and taller rectangles with area 1: width 1 height 1, width 1/2 height 2, width 1/10 height 10. The limit is a 'spike' with zero width but area 1.

46G.idea: Measuring, adding up and differentiating still make sense when the values are themselves points in infinite-dimensional spaces.
46G.entry: Hard to make faithful. Glimpse: average a whole family of curves (say each day's temperature graph over a month) to get one 'average curve'; the answer is itself a function.

46H.idea: Some spaces of functions can be multiplied as well as added, and the size of a product is at most the product of sizes.
46H.entry: Check with polynomials on [0,1] that the biggest value of f·g is at most (biggest of f)·(biggest of g). Find an example where it is strictly less.

46J.idea: In commutative algebras of functions, the space can be rebuilt from the algebra: points correspond to ways of 'evaluating'.
46J.entry: Hard to reach. Glimpse: the rule 'plug in x=2' turns polynomials into numbers and respects + and ×. Find all such rules: each one secretly is a point.

46K.idea: Algebras with a 'mirror' operation, like complex conjugation, where the mirror of a product is the product of mirrors reversed.
46K.entry: Conjugate complex numbers: check that the conjugate of zw is (conj z)(conj w) and z·conj z is never negative. Then try transposing 2x2 matrices: the order flips.

46L.idea: Algebras of operators, modelling quantum observables, where order of multiplication matters and size is tightly linked to algebra.
46L.entry: Hard to reach faithfully. Glimpse: multiply the 2x2 matrices for 'flip' and 'rotate 90°' in both orders and see AB ≠ BA, the seed of quantum uncertainty.

46M.idea: Building new function spaces by combining old ones (tensor products, limits) and tracking how constructions fit together systematically.
46M.entry: Hard to reach. Glimpse: a 2-by-3 times table grid built from (a,b) and (x,y,z) is a 'tensor product'; check which 2x3 grids of numbers arise this way.

46N.idea: Functional analysis gives tools for physics, economics, signal processing and more by treating functions as points.
46N.entry: Compress a short list of 8 numbers by keeping only the averages and differences of pairs (a Haar step), then rebuild it. Dropping small differences barely changes the signal.

46S.idea: Doing functional analysis with unusual number systems: p-adic numbers, infinitesimals, fuzzy sets, or only constructive proofs.
46S.entry: Glimpse via p-adic size: call a number small if divisible by a high power of 2. Then 1, 2, 4, 8, ... shrinks to 0, and 1+2+4+8+... 'equals' -1.

46T.idea: Solving nonlinear equations where the unknown is a whole function, using fixed points and infinite-dimensional calculus.
46T.entry: Find a function equal to its own running area plus 1: start with f=1, repeatedly replace f by 1 + area under f from 0 to x, and watch e^x appear.

47A.idea: A linear operator transforms vectors while respecting addition and scaling; its eigenvalues tell its essential behaviour.
47A.entry: Apply the matrix [[2,1],[1,2]] to many arrows on grid paper. Most arrows turn, but (1,1) and (1,-1) just stretch. Find the stretch factors.
